title: Dissolving self
content_html:
Dissolving self

In cognitive neuroscience, the self is not a single entity but an emergent process - a narrative construct built by memory, perception, and prediction. The brain continuously generates a self-model to organize experience and guide behavior, and memory contributes by maintaining continuity across time - the illusion that “I am the same person I was yesterday.” When this continuity weakens (e.g. during meditation, trauma, psychedelics, or deep sleep), the sense of self dissolves, revealing the underlying flux of sensory and emotional experience. In predictive processing terms, the self is a high-level prior - a model that integrates interoceptive (bodily), exteroceptive (sensory), and proprioceptive (movement) signals into a coherent “me.” When precision weighting shifts (the brain becomes less confident in that model), the boundary between self and world blurs.

In phenomenology, the dissolving self represents a transition from subject–object duality to pure awareness: consciousness not as a container but as an intentional arc - always already entangled with the world. The self dissolves when awareness stops clinging to distinctions between observer and observed - a direct experiential insight echoed in Zen and Advaita Vedanta. The “I” that perceives is not a fixed entity but an ongoing act of perceiving. When that act ceases to reference itself, only perception remains.

In Buddhist psychology, this is the realization of anattā (non-self): The self is seen as a bundle of aggregates (skandhas) - form, feeling, perception, volition, and consciousness - none of which is permanent or independent. Meditation allows direct insight into their impermanence, leading to non-identification: sensations arise and pass without the illusion of “I” who owns them. This dissolving is not annihilation but liberation - the disappearance of clinging, aversion, and the illusion of separateness.

When the self dissolves, the world does not vanish - it becomes intimate.

If we map this into a memory × nature triad:

Select: the self filters - choosing which sensations or memories “belong” to it.
Change: the self reorganizes experience through feedback loops of prediction and correction.
Reconstruct: memory and perception co-create the sense of continuity.

In the dissolving self, these loops relax - boundaries become porous, as in ecological systems where individual identity is secondary to interdependence (mycorrhizal networks, water cycles, neural synchrony). The self dissolves back into the larger field of being-memory-nature, where every pattern is transient yet recursively renewed.

In art, the dissolving self manifests as gestures that lose reference to the individual hand and instead reveal process, flow states where the artist becomes the movement itself. It’s the creative moment when authorship evaporates, and creation feels self-arising. The dissolving self is not the end of identity but its dynamic transparency.

It reveals that the self is an organizing fiction, necessary but not absolute. Dissolution is part of the same cycle as reconstruction - echoing the Select → Change → Reconstruct triad. Memory does not belong to the self; the self belongs to memory. The self is the trace memory leaves as it looks at itself - dissolving is remembering - without the “rememberer.”

The Dissolving Self

2025-10-09

The notion of a self that can dissolve is paradoxical: how can that which is presumed central disappear? Yet the dissolving self is not absence, but transformation - a thinning of boundaries, a re-turning to the source. In exploring this theme, we trace the interplay of memory, perception, and embodiment; philosophy and neuroscience; spiritual insight and ecological resonance. The dissolving self is neither destruction nor escape, but a revealing of what lies beneath the illusion of solidity.

Contemporary cognitive science often distinguishes multiple “selves.” The narrative self is the autobiographical story - the remembered “I” over time. The minimal self refers to moment-to-moment embodied consciousness: the sense of being an experiencer here now. The extended self projects into future goals, social identities, symbols. The “self” is not a singular substance but a process of integration across sensory, interoceptive, mnemonic, and predictive layers. It is a dynamic attractor in the brain’s generative model of the world.

From a critical perspective, the self is a useful fiction - a summary point for fluid processes. Hume famously argued for the absence of a fixed self behind perceptions; more recently, James Giles frames the self as a “constructed or condensed self-image” rather than an enduring core. Neural and philosophical accounts alike find no centralized “self node” in the brain. Thus the self is less a locus and more a narrative hologram, projected by memory and expectation.

In psychology, the term ego dissolution denotes a conscious state marked by a lowering or loss of the sense of self-boundaries, often accompanied by unity or oneness. Such states can arise in mystical experience, deep meditation, or with psychedelics. These experiences tend to reduce self-related thoughts, interrupt the narrative stream, diminish body-ownership sensations, blur spatial location, and lower minimal self-awareness.

In contemplative traditions, the dissolving self is cultivated gradually by practices such as insight meditation (vipassanā), self-inquiry, and nondual contemplation. Mindfulness of impermanence and the emptiness of phenomena weakens identification with self-structures. Buddhism’s doctrine of anattā (non-self) holds that there is no permanent, independent self. The sense of self is a temporary aggregation of processes - none of which by themselves is “I.” Not all freedom from self is benign. In extreme dissociative or psychotic states, self-boundaries may collapse involuntarily, leading to alienation, disorientation, or anguish. Some testimonies speak of “dissolution” as devastating rather than liberating. Thus the context, preparation, and integration matter: the dissolving self is not always welcome, and must be approached with care.

Memory stitches the flow of experience into a coherent identity. The self is, in large measure, memory’s “self-image.” In the Select → Change → Reconstruct triad, memory plays the reconstructing role: selecting what persists, changing what fades, reconstructing continuity. When memory’s anchoring weakens, the self begins to dissolve. As self-boundaries soften, the separation between inner and outer melts. The dissolving self experiences interpenetration - the world not as “other,” but as a shared field. In ecological, mythic, or mystical imagery, the self flows into forests, rivers, organisms, stars. In this state, memory is not “mine” - memory is nature remembering itself.

Dissolution does not abolish memory, but resets its orientation. After the moment of self-dissolution, memory re-forms new patterns - less centered, more distributed, more relational. The artist returns to brush, the writer to page, but with a breath-trace of emptiness. The dissolving self gestures toward an ontology of nonduality: being that does not uphold subject–object split. In this vision, existence is a single unfolding. The self is a pattern in that unfolding, not the prime mover. Real freedom arises after one lets go of the self - because then there is no “owner” to be bound or opposed. Will and agency continue, but they are no longer tethered to a separate “I.”

If the self dissolves, what becomes the ground for ethics? One answer: compassion and interdependence. Without a separate self, harm to another is harm to oneself. Altruism is not a duty but a natural expression of interconnected being. There is risk: dissolution may breed passivity or nihilism unless the creative tension of responsibility remains.

~

Whilst the self acknowledges the past (how I became) it seems primarily concerned with the present (how I feel now). If Memory does not belong to the self, the self belongs to memory, then this suggests that memory itself is more concerned with the present and future than being an accurate record of the past? Ultimately, calling it ‘memory’ is to misname it?

In many respects, “memory” as we commonly use the word is a kind of linguistic illusion, a misnomer for something far more dynamic. In everyday language, memory is imagined as a storehouse - a static repository of past impressions.

But cognitive neuroscience, especially since the 1990s, has shown that there are no stable neural “files” waiting to be retrieved. Hippocampal-cortical dynamics show that recollection is a reconstruction, not retrieval: the hippocampus binds together distributed cortical traces anew each time. Reconsolidation research confirms that each act of remembering opens a memory to change; every recall is re-encoding in the present. Thus, memory is not a photograph of the past but an act of prediction using past experience - a kind of simulation engine biased toward the now and what might come next. In this view, the self’s apparent orientation to the present (“how I feel now”) is actually memory at work - constantly updating models of the world to minimize surprise and maintain coherence.

The Free-Energy Principle and predictive processing frameworks dissolve any clean division between perception, memory, and imagination. All are temporal inference - the brain predicting incoming signals based on prior experience, then adjusting when prediction errors occur.

  • Perception = immediate prediction of the present.
  • Memory = prediction informed by longer temporal context.
  • Imagination or planning = prediction extended into future scenarios.

Seen this way, memory is the continuous act of maintaining temporal coherence. It is less a record of “what happened” and more a model of how reality tends to unfold - continuously updated by new data. So memory is concerned with the present and future; the past survives only as pattern, not archive.

If we flip the statement:

“Memory does not belong to the self - the self belongs to memory”

then the self becomes a momentary configuration within an ongoing reconstructive process. The self acknowledges the past because it must maintain narrative continuity - but that continuity is fabricated by memory’s need for coherence. The self feels rooted in the present because memory’s predictions are optimised for the now - to stabilise ongoing perception. Thus, the self is memory’s local equilibrium - the spot where prediction and sensation balance momentarily before both evolve.

Etymologically, memoria (Latin) means remembrance - but our modern sense implies something stored, retrieved, owned. That’s an artifact of written culture and storage metaphors (tablets, books, computers). A more accurate term might be: remembrance-as-process, or temporal inference, or adaptive continuity - but none of these have the resonance of “memory.” So language lags behind cognition; we keep the wrong noun for the right phenomenon. Perhaps “memory” is to mind what “sunrise” is to astronomy - a phenomenologically apt but physically inverted description. When we call it memory, we mean the living process of coherence: the ongoing stitching of experience into a self-consistent now. But the word freezes what is fluid - it turns the wave into an object.

“The word freezes what is fluid - it turns the wave into an object.” can be read almost as a poetic paraphrase of quantum measurement theory and the observer effect. In quantum mechanics, physical systems exist as superpositions - overlapping probabilities that describe all possible states. Only when a measurement occurs (an act of observation or interaction) does that wavefunction appear to “collapse” into a specific outcome.Before measurement: the system is fluid, indeterminate, holistic - a wave of potentialities. After measurement: it becomes discrete, definite - an object with properties. So when we say “the word freezes what is fluid”, we’re describing something analogous: Language is measurement. Naming collapses the field of possibilities into a single semantic outcome.

In this sense, every definition is a form of epistemic collapse - a necessary reduction that allows us to communicate, but at the cost of erasing uncertainty and relational nuance. Every noun is an act of measurement. Every sentence collapses a wave.

Cognitive linguistics shows a similar mechanism, the mind’s pre-verbal experience - raw perception, emotion, memory flux - is continuous and multidimensional. Language discretizes this continuum into categories and objects:

  • “Tree” isolates an instance from the forest’s fluid web.
  • “I” isolates a temporary configuration of sensations and memories.
  • “Memory” isolates an ongoing reconstructive process and freezes it into a noun.

This is a kind of semantic decoherence, where meaning collapses into stable symbols so communication can occur - but something essential (context, continuity, uncertainty) is lost. Thus, naming is both an act of creation and reduction - like a quantum measurement that brings forth a world, but never the whole one.

Phenomenology, Zen, and even Derrida’s deconstruction echo the same insight: language is the “house of Being,” but also its prison - it both reveals and conceals. Concepts are śūnyatā made visible - form arising from emptiness. Words make things appear, but what appears is never the whole. Each sign points beyond itself; meaning is always deferred (différance), never complete - the semantic wave is never truly collapsed. So when we speak of memory, we simultaneously manifest it and misname it - turning process into object, verb into noun, flow into thing.

Some modern interpretations of quantum theory (e.g. von Neumann–Wigner, QBism, relational quantum mechanics) emphasize that observation and information exchange are not passive but participatory. In these views, observation is the act that defines the observed - just as in cognition, attention constructs experience. memory behaves quantum-like: each recall is a measurement that alters the remembered state; every “collapse” is temporary and reversible; and the act of remembering changes what is remembered. Memory is the observer’s shadow, dancing on the surface of possibility. Even in ecosystems, measurement and naming have physical consequences. Naming a river, defining its “banks,” or charting its flow alters how we manage it - we impose boundaries upon a system that is intrinsically open and self-renewing.

So, across scales - from quantum fields to cognitive fields - the act of fixing identity is an act of freezing motion.

Qbism

QBism (short for Quantum Bayesianism) is one of the most philosophically intriguing interpretations of quantum mechanics, especially if we’re thinking about observation, meaning, and the role of the observer. It reinterprets quantum mechanics as a theory about an agent’s personal expectations - not about objective physical states that exist independently of observation.

In QBism, the quantum state (the wavefunction, ψ) does not represent a physical wave or an objective property of a system. Instead, it represents an agent’s personal degrees of belief about the outcomes of possible measurements. These beliefs follow the rules of Bayesian probability - they update when new information (a measurement result) arrives. So, the wavefunction collapse is not a physical event in the world, but a mental update - the observer’s beliefs changing upon interaction.

In classical physics, the observer is detached: they measure a world that exists independently of them. In QBism, observation is participation - the observer and the observed co-create the event. Each measurement outcome is personal - it is the agent’s experience of the world. But because all agents share the same mathematical rules (quantum probabilities), their subjective experiences remain consistent enough to build intersubjective science.

A measurement is not a revelation of pre-existing facts,
but an act that brings about a new fact for the observer. Fuchs & Schack, 2014

Bayesian probability treats probability not as frequency (objective chance), but as degree of belief. You begin with a prior belief, perform an experiment, and then update to a posterior belief according to new evidence. In QBism, quantum probabilities play this exact role. The Born rule (which calculates the probability of measurement outcomes) is reinterpreted as a coherence constraint - a consistency rule for how rational agents should update beliefs in light of quantum events. The Born rule is not a law of nature, but a law of rational expectation.

QBism replaces the idea of a pre-existing world with a participatory one. The universe is not a static object being watched - it is a field of potential experiences that crystallize through interaction.

  • Before measurement: possibilities (potential experiences).
  • Measurement: interaction → new experience (fact for that agent).
  • After: the agent updates their model of the world.

Reality becomes plural and relational, not monolithic - similar to Relational Quantum Mechanics (Rovelli, 1996), but with a more explicitly subjective twist. QBism revives the old insight (from William James’s radical empiricism and John Wheeler’s participatory universe) that the observer is not outside the cosmos but within it - shaping it by perceiving it. This makes it conceptually resonant with our framework of memory, self, and reconstruction:

  • Measurement → Selection (collapse, attention)
  • Update → Change (belief revision)
  • Reconstruction → Rebuild model of reality

The word freezes what is fluid - it turns the wave into an object mirrors QBism’s view that language and observation are acts of creation, not passive reflections.

Summary

Concept Classical Physics Quantum Mechanics (Copenhagen) QBism
Wavefunction ψ Objective physical reality Objective probabilities for measurement outcomes Subjective degrees of belief
Measurement Reveals a pre-existing property Collapses the wavefunction Creates a new personal experience
Probability Frequency or chance in the world Statistical rule of outcomes Agent’s Bayesian expectation
Observer Detached Causes collapse Participant; updates beliefs
Reality Independent, objective Partly dependent on observation Fully participatory and relational
